Tool-use agents fail in a specific way: they learn the shape of the environments they were trained on and then break on real APIs. The obvious fix is more training tasks. A large-scale study from a Google DeepMind team (Andrew Szot, Samira Abnar, Omar Attia, Abbas Kazerouni and colleagues) suggests that is the wrong lever.

The work introduces **SynthAPI**, a generation pipeline that explicitly controls the diversity of synthetic tool-use environments along three axes: the **tools** available, the **tasks** to solve, and the **databases** the tools operate on. By systematically varying those controls across **458,752 tasks and 849 trained models** in four size classes, the authors derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use generalization from the scale and composition of the synthesized environments.

## What the law says

The headline finding is a substitution effect. As the data budget grows, **scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than simply increasing the number of tasks** — a second agent talking to the same APIs learns almost nothing new, no matter how many instructions you vary. And **increasing data complexity yields larger gains**: environments with more moving pieces transfer better than simple ones.

Following those lessons produces agents that beat models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation, and the gains hold **across four evaluation benchmarks**.

This is the same family of lesson the industry keeps relearning about pretraining data — but here it is measured at the level of API surfaces and database schemas, which is where enterprise agent deployments actually live. If your training corpus exercises a hundred functions across three schemas, no amount of prompt variation on those functions produces an agent that generalizes to a new CRM.

The practical read is uncomfortable for teams that scale agent data by scaling task lists: the binding constraint is probably the number of distinct *environments* in your synthetic generator, and the pipeline you need to build to widen it, not the volume of prompts you can template.

The paper is on [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37648) under ID 2610.37648, submitted 27 October 2026.
